Task 8.1D — Sydney Housing Price Prediction and Decision Support System¶

SIT307 Machine Learning — ML Mini Project

Part Content
1 Problem definition, suburb selection, data collection and data quality
2 Exploratory analysis, outliers, feature engineering
3 Ridge regression vs. random forest vs. gradient boosting with nested k-fold CV
4 Investigation of the five largest prediction errors
5 Streamlit app (app/app.py) and reflection

Files needed in the same folder: Sydney_Housing_Data.xlsx (the collected dataset) and housing_features.py (the shared feature pipeline, also used by the app). Libraries: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, openpyxl, joblib. Run with Restart & Run All; Part 3 takes about 3–5 minutes.

Part 1: Problem Definition and Data Collection¶

1.1 The prediction problem¶

The task is a supervised regression problem: predict the sale price of a residential property in Sydney from its characteristics (location, property type, size, features and the agent's description). A real estate agency can use such a model as a decision-support tool, for example to sense-check an appraisal, to set a price guide, or to show a buyer whether an asking price is reasonable for comparable properties.

The model is trained on recently sold properties (not asking prices), so the target reflects what buyers actually paid.

1.2 Suburb selection and motivation¶

Mount Druitt (2770) Cabramatta (2166) Vaucluse (2030)
Location Outer western Sydney, ≈ 38 km from the CBD South-western Sydney, ≈ 25 km from the CBD Eastern Suburbs, ≈ 6.5 km from the CBD, on the harbour
Market Entry-level, first-home buyers and investors Mid-range, strong owner-occupier and investor demand Prestige / luxury market
What drives value Large blocks, granny-flat potential, rental yield; Westfield, station and hospital nearby Train station, Southeast Asian business and food district ("Little Vietnam"), higher-density zoning near the centre Harbour and ocean views, beaches, scarce land, prestige schools
Why I would consider buying here Affordable way to enter the Sydney market and own land Familiar culture and a large Southeast Asian community; good transport and value for money Aspirational, long-term benchmark of the top end of the market

(Distances are approximate straight-line distances from the suburb centre to the Sydney CBD.)

✏️ Personalise this row before submitting — the task asks why you would consider buying in each suburb.

The three suburbs were chosen because they represent substantially different housing markets: they differ in distance to the CBD, demographic profile, accessibility (rail-based western suburbs vs. harbourside east) and price level. This variety makes the prediction problem harder but more realistic, because the model has to learn that the same house is worth very different amounts in different places.

1.3 How suburb features may influence price¶

  • Location / suburb is expected to dominate. Most of a Sydney property's value is in the land, and land value depends on proximity to the CBD, water and amenities. A 4-bedroom house in Vaucluse should sell for several times the price of a similar house in Mount Druitt.
  • Property type matters because a house includes its own land while a unit or townhouse (strata) shares a parcel with other owners. The house–unit gap should be largest where land is most expensive (Vaucluse).
  • Size (bedrooms, bathrooms, car spaces, land size) increases price in every suburb, but the value of an extra bedroom or square metre should be higher in expensive suburbs, which suggests suburb × size interactions.
  • Suburb-specific features matter differently: views and water proximity in Vaucluse; train-station access, zoning and development potential in Cabramatta; granny flats, rental income and block size in Mount Druitt.

1.4 The collected dataset¶

Each sold listing was opened on realestate.com.au or domain.com.au and its details were copied manually into Sydney_Housing_Data.xlsx. Recorded fields: sale price (target), sale date, sale method, property type, bedrooms, bathrooms, car spaces, land size, building size, year built, six Yes/No features (pool, air-con, renovated, views, study, outdoor space), agency and the full agent description (text data). Data-entry decisions were logged in a Notes column.

1.5 Data quality, collection challenges, bias and limitations¶

Quality and missing information

  • The dataset meets the brief: 101 sold properties (Mount Druitt 31, Cabramatta 36, Vaucluse 34). Price, sale date, type, bedrooms and bathrooms are complete.
  • Year built (98% missing) and building size (83% missing) are rarely published on listing pages, so they cannot be used as features. Bedrooms and bathrooms are used as size proxies instead.
  • Land size is 63% missing, but most of this is structural: strata units and townhouses have no private land (the "site area" shown is the whole complex, which was deliberately not recorded as land). Among houses, 15–24% are missing land size.
  • Sale method is "Not stated" for 59% of sales, so it is too incomplete to use. 13 listings show no agency.
  • The Yes/No features were coded from the agent's description. A "No" often means "not mentioned", not "not present", so these flags are noisy.

Errors and anomalies found

  • ID 79 (Cabramatta unit) has the listing URL of ID 72 (a Vaucluse house). The wrong link was already in the raw copied text, so the URL for ID 79 needs to be re-checked; its other values match the Cabramatta page.
  • Three multi-dwelling sales (ID 1: two adjoining lots on an R4 development site; ID 35: four apartments sold together; ID 39: two dwellings) are not comparable to single-property sales.
  • Some land sizes were taken from the description text rather than the listing header, and some listings appeared on both portals (same price), which needed de-duplication.

Challenges during collection

  • Manual copy-and-paste from two portals with different layouts was slow and error-prone (several pages were pasted 2–3 times into the raw text file).
  • Many sales show "price withheld" or "contact agent", so they could not be used. This was most noticeable at the top end of the market.
  • Agent descriptions are long, inconsistent marketing text, and realestate.com.au adds AI-generated "highlights" that may not match the property.

Potential sources of bias

  • Selection bias: sales with withheld prices are excluded. These are more common in the prestige market, so Vaucluse's highest sales are probably under-represented.
  • Time-window bias: Vaucluse sales span May 2025 – Sep 2026, Cabramatta Oct 2025 – Sep 2026, but Mount Druitt only May – Sep 2026. Differences between suburbs are partly mixed with differences in timing.
  • Composition bias: Cabramatta's sample is 64% strata, Mount Druitt's 58%, Vaucluse's 50%. Raw suburb medians therefore compare different mixes of property types (see Part 2).
  • Marketing bias: descriptions are written to sell, so positive features are emphasised and negatives (main-road noise, poor condition) are left out.

Limitations for validity

  • About 100 rows across 3 suburbs and 5 property types leaves only 13–23 properties in each suburb × segment group, which limits model complexity and the reliability of any estimate.
  • Because only three suburbs are covered, the model cannot generalise to other suburbs, and suburb-level information (such as distance to the CBD) is indistinguishable from the suburb itself.
  • Prices range from $310k to $22.4M (72×). Errors on prestige homes will dominate dollar-based metrics.

Findings. Prices are strongly right-skewed (skewness 2.80): the mean ($2.70M) is more than double the median ($1.10M) because of a small number of Vaucluse sales above $10M. Taking the log reduces skewness to 0.95, but the log-price histogram is multi-modal: each suburb forms its own cluster, and Vaucluse barely overlaps the other two. Decision: model log(price) in Part 3 so that a $22M sale does not dominate training, then convert predictions back to dollars.

Findings.

  • Vaucluse is a separate market. Its median house ($7.95M) costs about 7× a Mount Druitt house ($1.11M), while its median unit ($1.40M) costs about 3× a Mount Druitt unit. The house premium is highest where land is most expensive.
  • Raw suburb medians are misleading. Cabramatta's overall median ($553k) is lower than Mount Druitt's ($840k), but only because 64% of Cabramatta sales are units. Comparing like with like, Cabramatta houses ($1.65M) are worth about 50% more than Mount Druitt houses, while units in the two suburbs sell for nearly the same price (≈ $0.48–0.50M). Suburb and property type have to be considered together.
  • Variation differs by suburb: Mount Druitt is the most uniform (CV 0.45). Cabramatta's CV (1.20) is inflated by the $8.05M development site (ID 1).
  • Bedrooms increase price in all three suburbs, but the slope is steepest in Vaucluse. In the log-linear fits, each extra bedroom adds roughly 40% in Mount Druitt, 54% in Cabramatta and 81% in Vaucluse (single dwellings only). This supports including suburb × size interactions in Part 3.

Findings.

  • The sampling window is uneven (bottom chart). Early sales are almost all Vaucluse, and Mount Druitt only appears from May 2026. Any overall price trend is therefore confounded with suburb: across all data, later sales look cheaper (Spearman −0.21 between sale date and log price) simply because the late sales are mostly from Mount Druitt.
  • Within comparable groups, the trend is upward but weak: Cabramatta units rose from a median of $0.43M (2025) to $0.49M (2026 H1) and $0.52M (2026 H2), and Vaucluse units from $1.39M to $1.80M. These groups contain only 1–16 sales each, so the movement cannot be separated from differences in the properties sold.
  • Market movement over 17 months is small compared with the gaps between suburbs and property types. A time variable (DaysSinceStart) is included as a feature, but it is not expected to be a major driver.

2.4 Unusual observations and potential outliers¶

An outlier is judged within its own suburb and segment, because a $10M sale is typical in Vaucluse but extreme in Mount Druitt. A robust z-score (median and MAD) on log price is used, with |z| > 2.5 flagged. Implausible feature values are also flagged.

In [10]:
# Outliers are judged within comparable groups (suburb x segment) using a robust z-score on log price,
# because a $10M sale is normal in Vaucluse but extreme in Mount Druitt.
def robust_z(s):
    med = s.median()
    mad = (s - med).abs().median() * 1.4826
    return (s - med) / mad if mad > 0 else s * 0

df["RobustZ"] = df.groupby(["Suburb", "Segment"], observed=True)["LogPrice"].transform(robust_z)

# Also flag implausible feature values
df["FeatureFlag"] = ""
df.loc[df["Cars"] > 6, "FeatureFlag"] += "cars>6; "
df.loc[df["Bedrooms"] > 7, "FeatureFlag"] += "beds>7; "
df.loc[df["MultiDwelling"] == 1, "FeatureFlag"] += "multi-dwelling; "

flagged = df[(df["RobustZ"].abs() > 2.5) | (df["FeatureFlag"] != "")]
display(flagged[["ID", "Suburb", "Type", "Price", "Bedrooms", "Bathrooms", "Cars", "Land_m2", "RobustZ", "FeatureFlag"]]
        .sort_values("RobustZ", ascending=False)

No sale price looks like a data-entry error, so all 101 rows are kept (removing rows would also drop the dataset below the required 100). The log target, the MultiDwelling flag and capping limit how much these rows affect the model. In Part 3, results will also be checked with the three multi-dwelling sales removed.

2.5 The three variables expected to influence price most (stated before feature engineering)¶

  1. Suburb (location). Land value is set by location: distance to the CBD, water, transport and the area's socio-economic profile. Part 1 and the box plots show prices ranging from entry-level to prestige across the three suburbs.
  2. Property type (house vs. strata). A house owns its land outright, while a unit owns only a share of a strata parcel. In Sydney, land is where most of the value lies, so type should create a large price step within every suburb.
  3. Bedrooms (size of the dwelling). Building size is mostly missing, so bedrooms is the best available measure of how much house is being bought. More bedrooms also usually means a larger block and more bathrooms and parking.

These are expected to interact. The value of being a house, and of each extra bedroom, should be much higher in Vaucluse than in Mount Druitt.

2.6 Feature engineering¶

Features were engineered to (a) make incomplete raw fields usable, (b) represent the drivers identified above more directly, and (c) extract information from the agent descriptions (text data).

Group Feature Why
Target LogPrice Reduces skew; errors become relative (%) rather than dollar-based
Type / land IsHouse Collapses 5 types into the land-owning vs. strata distinction (rare types: Villa n = 2, Semi/Duplex n = 1)
LogLand, LandMissing Strata = 0 m² (no private land). Missing house land is filled with that suburb's house median, with a flag so the model knows it was filled
Size Rooms, BathPerBed, CarsCapped Size proxies, because building size is 83% missing. Car spaces are capped at 6 to limit the multi-lot sale
Quality AmenityScore Count of the six Yes/No features. Individually they are noisy, together they signal a higher-spec property
Location DistCBD_km External, suburb-level information (straight-line distance to the CBD)
Time DaysSinceStart Captures market movement across the 17-month window
Unusual sale MultiDwelling Marks the three multi-dwelling sales
Text kw_water, kw_luxury, kw_devpot, kw_station, kw_investor, kw_reno, DescWords Keyword flags from the agent description for views/water, luxury language, development potential, train access, investor/first-home-buyer language, renovation, and description length
In [11]:
fe = df.copy()

# --- 1. Clean and encode collected features ------------------------------------------
yes_no = ["Pool", "Air Con", "Renovated", "Views", "Study", "Outdoor Space"]
for c in yes_no:
    fe[c] = (fe[c] == "Yes").astype(int)
fe["AmenityScore"] = fe[yes_no].sum(axis=1)                      # how many listed extras

fe["IsHouse"] = (fe["Segment"] == "House / duplex").astype(int)   # owns land vs strata share
fe["CarsCapped"] = fe["Cars"].fillna(fe.groupby(["Suburb", "Segment"], observed=True)["Cars"].transform("median")).clip(upper=6)

# Land: 0 for strata (no private land), suburb-median of houses for houses with missing land, + missing flag
fe["LandMissing"] = (fe["IsHouse"].eq(1) & fe["Land_m2"].isna()).astype(int)
house_land_med = fe[fe["IsHouse"] == 1].groupby("Suburb", observed=True)["Land_m2"].median()
fe["LandFilled"] = np.where(fe["IsHouse"] == 0, 0,
                            fe["Land_m2"].fillna(fe["Suburb"].map(house_land_med).astype(float)))
fe["LogLand"] = np.log1p(fe["LandFilled"])

# Size proxies (building size is 83% missing, so rooms stand in for floor area)
fe["Rooms"] = fe["Bedrooms"] + fe["Bathrooms"]
fe["BathPerBed"] = fe["Bathrooms"] / fe["Bedrooms"]

# --- 2. Location (external data: straight-line distance from suburb centre to Sydney CBD) ---
DIST_CBD_KM = {"Vaucluse": 6.5, "Cabramatta": 25.4, "Mount Druitt": 37.7}
fe["DistCBD_km"] = fe["Suburb"].astype(str).map(DIST_CBD_KM)

# --- 3. Time ------------------------------------------------------------------------
fe["DaysSinceStart"] = (fe["SaleDate"] - fe["SaleDate"].min()).dt.days
fe["SaleQuarter"] = fe["SaleDate"].dt.quarter

# --- 4. Text features from the agent description ---------------------------------------
text = fe["Description"].fillna("").str.lower()
KEYWORDS = {
    "kw_water":    r"harbour|ocean|beach|water view|bay\b|waterfront",
    "kw_luxury":   r"luxur|prestige|architect|designer|bespoke|resort|grand",
    "kw_devpot":   r"develop|granny|dual occ|subdivi|\br4\b|\br3\b|stca|zoning",
    "kw_station":  r"station|train",
    "kw_investor": r"invest|rental|\brent\b|first home",
    "kw_reno":     r"renovat|refurbish|brand new|newly|updated",
}
for k, pat in KEYWORDS.items():
    fe[k] = text.str.contains(pat, regex=True).astype(int)
fe["DescWords"] = text.str.split().str.len()

engineered = ["IsHouse", "LogLand", "LandMissing", "Rooms", "BathPerBed", "CarsCapped", "AmenityScore",
              "DistCBD_km", "DaysSinceStart", "MultiDwelling"] + list(KEYWORDS) + ["DescWords"]
fe[["ID", "Suburb"] + engineered].head()

Text features: how often keywords appear, and the price gap within suburbs¶

The "within-suburb price gap" compares the mean suburb-adjusted log price of listings with and without the keyword, expressed as a percentage.

In [12]:
# How often does each keyword appear per suburb, and is it linked to price *within* a suburb?
kw = list(KEYWORDS)
prev = fe.groupby("Suburb", observed=True)[kw].mean().mul(100).round(0)

fe["LogPrice_within"] = fe["LogPrice"] - fe.groupby("Suburb", observed=True)["LogPrice"].transform("mean")
prem = {}
for k in kw:
    g = fe.groupby(k)["LogPrice_within"].mean()
    prem[k] = (np.exp(g.get(1, np.nan) - g.get(0, np.nan)) - 1) * 100 if len(g) == 2 else np.nan
out = prev.T
out["Within-suburb price gap (%)"] = pd.Series(prem).round(0)
display(out.rename(columns=str))
Suburb Mount Druitt Cabramatta Vaucluse Within-suburb price gap (%)
kw_water 0.0 0.0 91.0 17.0
kw_luxury 6.0 25.0 59.0 110.0
kw_devpot 26.0 8.0 15.0 89.0

Findings. The text shows how agents market each suburb differently. Water and beach words appear in 91% of Vaucluse descriptions and never elsewhere, while train-station words appear in about 80% of western-Sydney listings and never in Vaucluse. As a result, these two flags mostly repeat the suburb. Investor / first-home-buyer language marks cheaper stock (−42% within suburbs), and luxury language (+110%) and development potential (+89%) mark more expensive stock. Part of this gap is because these words appear mainly in house listings, so the text features overlap with IsHouse.

2.7 Did the features behave as expected?¶

Each feature is compared with log price in two ways. The first uses the whole dataset, where suburb differences dominate. The second is within each suburb: the average of the correlations calculated separately inside each suburb, which shows whether a feature adds information beyond location. The share of variance in log price explained by suburb and segment (η²) is also calculated.

In [13]:
# Which features carry signal? (a) over the whole dataset, (b) after removing the suburb effect.
cand = ["Bedrooms", "Bathrooms"] + engineered
y_all = fe["LogPrice"]

def within_spearman(col):
    # average of the Spearman correlations computed separately inside each suburb
    vals = [g[col].corr(g["LogPrice"], method="spearman") for _, g in fe.groupby("Suburb", observed=True)
            if g[col].nunique() > 1]
    return np.mean(vals) if vals else np.nan

res = pd.DataFrame({
    "Spearman (all)": fe[cand].corrwith(y_all, method="spearman"),
    "Spearman (within suburb)": pd.Series({c: within_spearman(c) for c in cand}),
    "Mutual info (all)": mutual_info_regression(fe[cand].fillna(0), y_all, random_state=0, n_neighbors=5),
}).round(3)
# Suburb itself, as share of variance in log price it explains (eta squared)
eta = lambda col: 1 - ((y_all - fe.groupby(col, observed=True)["LogPrice"].transform("mean"))**2).sum() / ((y_all - y_all.mean())**2).sum()
print(f"Variance in log price explained by Suburb alone:          {eta('Suburb'):.2f}")
print(f"Variance in log price explained by Segment alone:         {eta('Segment'):.2f}")
fe["Suburb_x_Segment"] = fe["Suburb"].astype(str) + " | " + fe["Segment"]
print(f"Variance in log price explained by Suburb x Segment:      {eta('Suburb_x_Segment'):.2f}")

res = res.sort_values("Spearman (within suburb)", key=abs, ascending=False, na_position="last")
display(res.fillna("constant within suburb"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6.5))
res[["Spearman (all)", "Spearman (within suburb)"]].astype(float).iloc[::-1].plot.barh(ax=ax, color=["#BBBBBB", "#3A86A8"])
ax.axvline(0, c="k", lw=.8)
ax.set_title("Correlation with log(price): whole dataset vs within suburb")

2.8 Reflection: do the feature-engineering decisions match my initial understanding?¶

Mostly yes. The three chosen variables are confirmed, and the analysis made the picture more precise.

  • Suburb and property type together explain 89% of the variance in log price (suburb alone 48%, segment alone 46%). This confirms the first two choices and shows they work as a pair, not separately. The Cabramatta-vs-Mount-Druitt median reversal was the clearest evidence of this.
  • Size is confirmed as the third driver. Within suburbs, LogLand (0.86), Rooms (0.86), IsHouse (0.85) and Bedrooms (0.85) have the strongest correlations. These features are highly collinear because they all describe "a bigger house on its own land". This will matter in Part 3: linear models may give unstable coefficients, and regularisation or tree-based models may handle it better.
  • Engineered location features add nothing beyond the suburb label. DistCBD_km is constant within each suburb, so with only three suburbs it carries exactly the same information as the suburb label. The same is mostly true of kw_water and kw_station. They would only become useful if the dataset covered more suburbs. This was not obvious before the analysis.
  • Some text features add information within suburbs: luxury language (0.49), investor language (−0.40) and development potential (0.38). These capture quality and market segment that the structured fields miss, which supports using the agent descriptions. However, some of this overlaps with property type.
  • Weak or misleading features: BathPerBed, kw_reno and DaysSinceStart show little within-suburb signal. The time variable even changes sign (negative overall, positive within suburbs), which shows how the uneven sampling window could mislead a model that ignores suburb.

Implications for Part 3: model LogPrice; always include suburb together with IsHouse (and ideally their interaction); use one or two size features rather than all of them, or use regularisation; keep the better text flags; and treat suburb-level external features as unhelpful for this three-suburb dataset.

Part 3: Model Development and Evaluation¶

3.1 Model choice and expectations (written before training)¶

Three models were chosen from different modelling families. A simple baseline is included for reference: it predicts the median price of the property's suburb × segment (house or strata). A model is only useful if it beats this baseline.

Ridge regression Random forest Gradient boosting
Family Linear, regularised (parametric) Bagged decision trees (non-parametric) Boosted decision trees (sequential ensemble)
Why it suits this data Part 2 showed log price is close to additive in suburb, type and size. With only 101 rows, a low-variance model is attractive. The L2 penalty handles the collinear size features (Rooms, Bedrooms, LogLand, IsHouse) Learns suburb × type × size interactions and thresholds automatically. Averaging many trees on bootstrap samples reduces variance and is robust to the outliers found in Part 2 Often the most accurate model on tabular data. Each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones, so it can fit complex patterns
Weaknesses Interactions must be added by hand (suburb × IsHouse, suburb × Bedrooms). Assumes straight-line effects on log price. Extrapolates without limit for unusual inputs Cannot predict beyond the range of prices it has seen. Predictions are pulled towards leaf averages, so extremes shrink. Needs more data to fill its leaves Many hyperparameters. Its sequential fitting easily overfits small, noisy data. Like the random forest, it cannot extrapolate

Expectation: I expect Ridge regression to perform best, followed by the random forest, with gradient boosting last. With about 100 rows, a simple model with the right structure (log target plus hand-made interactions) should generalise better than tree ensembles that need many examples per region of the feature space. I expect gradient boosting to overfit the most.

All three models use the same 22 features from housing_features.py (Part 2 features; DistCBD_km and kw_station are dropped because they only repeat the suburb). They are trained on log(price). Ridge also standardises the features.

In [15]:
import time, warnings, joblib
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, RepeatedKFold, GridSearchCV, validation_curve
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

# Shared feature pipeline (also used by the Streamlit app) - see housing_features.py
from housing_features import HousingFeatures, load_raw

X_raw, price, full = load_raw("Sydney_Housing_Data.xlsx")
y = np.log(price)                                   # model log(price), as decided in Part 2
print("Model input:", X_raw.shape, "| features after engineering:", len(HousingFeatures().fit(X_raw).feature_names_))

def make_pipe(model, scale=False):
    steps = [("features", HousingFeatures(interactions=True))]
    if scale:
        steps.append(("scale", StandardScaler()))
    steps.append(("model", model))
    return Pipeline(steps)

INNER_CV = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)

MODELS = {
    "Ridge regression": GridSearchCV(
        make_pipe(Ridge(), scale=True),
        {"model__alpha": [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30]},
        cv=INNER_CV, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error"),
    "Random forest": GridSearchCV(
        make_pipe(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)),
        {"model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 3], "model__max_features": [0.33, 0.6, 1.0]},
        cv=INNER_CV, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error"),
    "Gradient boosting": GridSearchCV(
        make_pipe(GradientBoostingRegressor(subsample=0.8, random_state=0)),
        {"model__n_estimators": [100, 300], "model__learning_rate": [0.03, 0.1], "model__max_depth": [2, 3]},
        cv=INNER_CV, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error"),
}

3.2 Evaluation design: nested k-fold cross-validation¶

  • Outer loop: 5-fold cross-validation, repeated twice with different shuffles (10 test folds). This estimates how well each model predicts properties it has never seen. Repeating the CV reduces the luck of a single split, which matters with only about 20 properties per test fold.
  • Inner loop: a 5-fold grid search tunes the hyperparameters using only the outer-training rows, so tuning never sees the test fold. Feature imputation (median land and car spaces) is also fitted inside each fold through the pipeline.
  • Metrics: RMSE and R² on log price (≈ relative error, and the quantity being optimised). MAE in dollars (what a user experiences). MAPE and median absolute % error (comparable between cheap units and $20M houses). R² in dollars (dominated by expensive homes). Train vs test RMSE is reported to check for under- and overfitting.
In [17]:
# Nested cross-validation: the OUTER loop (5-fold, repeated twice with different shuffles) estimates
# performance on unseen properties; the INNER 5-fold grid search tunes hyperparameters using the
# outer-training rows only, so the reported scores are not optimistically biased by tuning.
OUTER_CV = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=2, random_state=42)
N_REPEATS = 2

def metrics(y_log_true, y_log_pred):
    p_true, p_pred = np.exp(y_log_true), np.exp(y_log_pred)
    ape = np.abs(p_pred - p_true) / p_true
    return {"RMSE (log)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_log_true, y_log_pred)),
            "R² (log)": r2_score(y_log_true, y_log_pred),
            "MAE ($)": mean_absolute_error(p_true, p_pred),
            "MAPE (%)": ape.mean() * 100,
            "Median APE (%)": np.median(ape) * 100,
            "R² ($)": r2_score(p_true, p_pred)}

rows, oof, chosen = [], {}, {}
# Baseline: predict the median log price of the property's suburb x segment (no ML)
seg = X_raw["Type"].isin(["House", "Semi/Duplex"]).map({True: "House", False: "Strata"})
group = X_raw["Suburb"] + "|" + seg

for name, model in {"Baseline (suburb x segment median)": None, **MODELS}.items():
    t0 = time.time()
    oof[name] = np.zeros((N_REPEATS, len(y)))
    chosen[name] = []
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(OUTER_CV.split(X_raw)):
        if model is None:
            med = y.iloc[tr].groupby(group.iloc[tr]).median()
            pred_tr = group.iloc[tr].map(med).values
            pred_te = group.iloc[te].map(med).fillna(y.iloc[tr].median()).values
        else:
            model.fit(X_raw.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr])
            pred_tr, pred_te = model.predict(X_raw.iloc[tr]), model.predict(X_raw.iloc[te])
            chosen[name].append(model.best_params_)
        oof[name][k // 5, te] = pred_te
        rows.append({"Model": name, "Fold": k, "Split": "train", **metrics(y.iloc[tr], pred_tr)})
        rows.append({"Model": name, "Fold": k, "Split": "test", **metrics(y.iloc[te], pred_te)})
    print(f"{name:38s} done in {time.time() - t0:5.1f}s")

cv_res = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Baseline (suburb x segment median)     done in   0.1s

Ridge regression                       done in  28.1s

Random forest                          done in 116.3s

Gradient boosting                      done in  69.5s

Gradient boosting:  {"{'model__learning_rate': 0.1, 'model__max_depth': 3, 'model__n_estimators': 100}": 4, "{'model__learning_rate': 0.03, 'model__max_depth': 3, 'model__n_estimators': 300}": 3, "{'model__learning_rate': 0.03, 'model__max_depth': 3, 'model__n_estimators': 100}": 2, "{'model__learning_rate': 0.1, 'model__max_depth': 3, 'model__n_estimators': 300}": 1}

Results. All three models beat the baseline on the log scale, so the features add real information beyond suburb and segment. The random forest is best on every metric: log RMSE 0.292 (≈ ±34% typical error), MAPE 19.5% and a median error of 13.4%. Gradient boosting comes second and Ridge comes third. The fold-to-fold standard deviation (≈ 0.09–0.10) is large compared with the gaps between models, so the ranking is not certain. The paired comparison below makes this clearer.

Two results stand out:

  • Ridge beats the baseline on the log scale but loses to it in dollars. Its dollar R² (0.43) and MAE ($1.17M) are worse than the baseline's. The cause is extrapolation: for ID 35 (four Vaucluse apartments sold as one, 11 bedrooms), the Vaucluse × bedrooms interaction projects a price of about $29M against an actual $6.45M. A linear model follows its slope for as far as the inputs go, and one such error dominates dollar metrics.
  • The tuned hyperparameters are unstable for Ridge. The inner search picked α = 0.01 in 5 folds but α = 10–30 in 3 folds. The random forest almost always chose max_features = 0.33, min_samples_leaf = 1. With 80 training rows, the best amount of regularisation depends heavily on which properties are in the fold.

Model behaviour.

  • Paired folds: the random forest beat Ridge on 7 of 10 folds, but gradient boosting beat it on only 5 of 10. The forest's advantage is consistent but modest, and gradient boosting is effectively tied with Ridge.
  • Where the errors are: every model is accurate for strata properties (median error 8–12% for the forest) and much worse for houses, especially Vaucluse houses (≈ 30%) and Cabramatta houses (≈ 27%). These groups have few sales, prices spread over a wide range, and value drivers (views, development zoning) that are only partly captured.
  • Shape of the errors (scatter plots): Ridge has the widest spread and the one extreme over-prediction. The tree models form a "ceiling" at about $12–13M. They under-predict every sale above $15M because a tree can only predict averages of prices it has seen in training.
  • Ridge is better than the forest for Cabramatta and Mount Druitt houses (20.0% vs 27.4%, and 13.4% vs 16.9%), where a smooth size effect works well. The forest wins clearly for strata properties and Vaucluse.

3.3 Underfitting, overfitting and model complexity¶

  • Baseline: underfits. Its train and test errors are both high (0.36 vs 0.39) and nearly equal, which is the signature of a model too simple to capture size or quality.
  • Ridge: well balanced, with a flat optimum. The validation curve is lowest at α ≈ 10–30 (CV RMSE ≈ 0.305) and almost flat as regularisation decreases. Train error keeps falling (0.27 → 0.19) while CV error rises slightly, so mild overfitting appears at very low α. The train–test gap in nested CV (0.13) is moderate.
  • Random forest: low train error but no overfitting penalty from depth. Trees deeper than about 4 levels hardly change CV error (≈ 0.30), even though train error falls to 0.11. Averaging 200 bootstrapped trees cancels most of the variance that deep single trees would add. The large train–test gap (0.18) is expected for a forest and is not harmful here.
  • Gradient boosting: the clearest overfitting. CV error is lowest at about 50 trees (≈ 0.31). After that, train error goes to almost zero (0.06 in nested CV, ≈ 0 at 400+ trees) while CV error rises slightly. It has the largest train–test gap (0.25) and the largest fold variance (sd 0.10). With so few rows, extra boosting rounds learn noise in individual sales.
  • Overall: more complexity helped up to a point (baseline → linear model → tree ensembles). Beyond that, the limiting factor is the information in the features and the number of examples, not model flexibility. All three models end up around 0.29–0.33.

3.4 Revisiting the expectations¶

My expectation was only partly supported.

  • ✗ Ridge was not the best. I underestimated how much the tree models gain from learning interactions and thresholds automatically. More importantly, I underestimated how badly a linear model behaves on rare, extreme inputs (the 11-bedroom multi-dwelling sale). On the log scale Ridge was competitive, but in dollar terms that extrapolation made it worse than the baseline.
  • ✓ Gradient boosting overfit the most, as predicted: the largest train–test gap, near-zero training error and the highest fold variance.
  • ✓ Small data limits every model. The three models are within about 0.04 log RMSE of each other, and the fold variability is larger than that gap.

3.5 Recommendation: Random forest¶

The random forest is recommended and deployed because it:

  1. has the lowest error on every metric in nested CV (log RMSE 0.292, MAPE 19.5%, MAE ≈ $0.90M, dollar R² 0.67) and beat Ridge on 7 of 10 paired folds;
  2. fails safely. It cannot produce absurd predictions such as Ridge's $29M, because its predictions stay within the range of prices it has seen. This is important in a public-facing app where users may enter unusual inputs;
  3. is stable to tune. The same hyperparameters were chosen in 7 of 10 folds, and performance is insensitive to tree depth;
  4. is robust to the multi-dwelling sales. Removing them did not improve accuracy on single dwellings (median error 11.9% with them vs 14.4% without), so they were kept.

Its main weakness, under-predicting the most expensive homes, is investigated in Part 4. The final forest was re-tuned on all 101 properties (max_features = 0.33, min_samples_leaf = 1) and saved for the app with an 80% error range calculated from its out-of-fold residuals: about −25% / +62% for houses and −19% / +18% for strata. The feature importances confirm the Part 2 findings: the Vaucluse × house and Vaucluse × bedrooms interactions dominate, followed by bathrooms, land size and water keywords.

Part 4: Investigating Prediction Failures¶

Each property is predicted by the recommended random forest when that property was in the test fold (out-of-fold predictions averaged over the two CV repeats), so every error is an honest error on an unseen property.

def rf_cv(extra=None):
    pipe = Pipeline([("features", HousingFeatures(extra_keywords=extra)),
                     ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_features=0.33, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1))])
    pred = np.zeros((N_REPEATS, len(y)))
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(OUTER_CV.split(X_raw)):
        pred[k // 5, te] = pipe.fit(X_raw.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]).predict(X_raw.iloc[te])
    return pred.mean(0)

4.1 The five largest errors¶

ID Property Actual → predicted Why the model failed
93 Vaucluse house, 5 bed, 680 m², 44A Wentworth Rd $22.41M → $8.11M (−64%) The record price in the data. Its value comes from a dual-frontage blue-chip street, direct views to the Opera House and Harbour Bridge, and a celebrated architect. None of these are recorded features. The forest cannot predict above the range of training prices it averages, and a near-identical structured comparable (ID 65: 5 bed, 694 m², pool) sold for only $7.5M.
95 Vaucluse house, 5 bed, 1,173 m², Dalley Ave $19.50M → $9.99M (−49%) Harbour panorama to the Opera House and Bridge on a very large block. A data-coding error made it worse: Views was recorded as "No" even though the description begins "Stunning Harbour Panoramas".
37 Vaucluse house, 5 bed, 775 m², New South Head Rd $16.00M → $8.93M (−44%) Panoramic harbour, Opera House and Bridge views, and a family-held home offered for the first time in 27 years. Its structured features (no pool, 2 car spaces) look below average for Vaucluse.
1 Cabramatta, two adjoining houses, 12 bed, 1,370 m² $8.05M → $1.62M (−80%) A record-price R4 development site in the Cabramatta CBD. The buyer paid for land and zoning, not for bedrooms. With only 3 multi-dwelling sales in the data, the forest has no similar examples, so it predicts like a large ordinary house.
72 Vaucluse house, 4 bed, 883 m², 20 Wentworth Rd $16.00M → $9.83M (−39%) A period residence ("Virginia") with uninterrupted harbour, Opera House and Bridge views on prestige Wentworth Road. Again, the location within the suburb and the view quality are not captured.

Common pattern. These five properties account for 49% of the model's total absolute dollar error, and all five are under-predicted. Four are Vaucluse houses whose descriptions mention views to the Opera House / Harbour Bridge. In the data, the six Vaucluse houses with such views have a median of $16.0M, compared with $6.86M for the other eleven. The kw_water flag treats harbour, ocean and beach as the same thing, which hides this premium. The largest percentage over-predictions (IDs 48 and 92, +88% and +85%) are the opposite case: Vaucluse houses with ocean views that the model valued like harbour-view homes.

Post-hoc check. Adding one keyword flag for "Opera House | Harbour Bridge" reduces the forest's log RMSE from 0.298 to 0.274 and raises dollar R² from 0.69 to 0.78. Even so, the four Vaucluse predictions in the top 5 only rise by $1.1–2.5M, and ID 1 does not change, because with six examples a tree still cannot reach $16–22M. This feature was designed after looking at the errors, so the improvement is optimistic. It was not added to the deployed model; it is a direction for future data collection.

4.2 Limitations and missing information¶

Limitations of the modelling approach

  • Tree ensembles cannot extrapolate and pull extreme prices towards the average, so the most valuable properties are always under-predicted. Linear models can extrapolate, but they did so wildly in Part 3. Neither family handles the top end well with about 100 rows.
  • Errors scale with price (see the box plot). Strata properties have median errors of about 8–12%, while houses in Vaucluse and Cabramatta vary by ±30% or more. A single error range for every property would be misleading, which is why the app reports separate ranges for houses and strata.
  • Few examples in key groups: 17 Vaucluse houses, 13 Cabramatta houses, 3 multi-dwelling sales and 2 villas. The model is effectively memorising each of these groups.
  • Keyword features are blunt. They detect words, not meaning. "Harbour view" and "walk to the harbour" look the same, and keyword flags cannot judge view quality.

Information that was unavailable but would likely help

  • Precise location within the suburb: street, side of the peninsula (harbour vs. ocean), distance to the water, station or CBD at property level, and lot frontage. Suburb-level location is too coarse for Vaucluse.
  • View quality and orientation (harbour/Opera House vs. ocean vs. none), ideally from photos or a geographic viewshed.
  • Internal floor area, year built, condition and renovation quality. These were 83–98% missing on listing pages, and bedrooms are only a rough proxy.
  • Zoning and development potential (e.g. R4 high density), lot dimensions and DA approvals. These drive development-site prices such as ID 1.
  • Sale context: auction vs. private treaty, days on market, number of bidders, and the prior sale price. Off-market and record sales depend on competition, not just features.
  • Listing photos. Image features could capture finish, architecture and outlook.

When to interpret predictions cautiously

  • Prestige properties (above about $10M), where the model's ceiling and ±30–60% errors apply.
  • Development sites and multi-dwelling sales, which are valued on land and zoning, not bedrooms.
  • Rare property types (villas, semis), very large homes (more than 7 bedrooms) or land sizes outside the training range.
  • Any suburb other than these three, and dates far outside May 2025 – Sep 2026, because market conditions change.
  • Listings whose structured fields disagree with the description, as in the Views error for ID 95.

Are some properties inherently harder to model? Yes. Standardised strata units are the easiest: they have many close comparables and value is driven by measurable features (bedrooms, bathrooms, parking). Unique, high-value houses and development sites are the hardest. Their prices depend on one-of-a-kind attributes (a specific view, street or zoning) and on buyer competition, and each has few or no comparables. Even a professional valuer relies on judgement for these properties, so a model trained on a small sample should be used only as a starting point.

Part 5: Final Deployment and Reflection¶

5.1 The web application¶

A Streamlit app (app/app.py) lets a user enter a property's details and receive a predicted sale price from the deployed random forest.

How it was developed

  1. One shared feature pipeline. All feature engineering lives in housing_features.py as a scikit-learn transformer (HousingFeatures). The notebook and the app therefore encode a property in exactly the same way, which avoids training/serving mismatch.
  2. Model packaging. The final pipeline (features + random forest) is saved with joblib to app/model.joblib, together with the 80% error-range values for houses and strata. If the file cannot be loaded (e.g. a different scikit-learn version on the server), the app re-trains it from the spreadsheet using app/train_model.py.
  3. Interface. A single form with input boxes for suburb, property type, bedrooms, bathrooms, car spaces, land size, sale date, multi-dwelling sale, six listed features (tick boxes) and an optional agent description. Clicking Estimate price builds one row of raw data, passes it through the saved pipeline, converts log price back to dollars and shows the estimate with its 80% likely range. The page uses the Open Sans font.
  4. Deployment. The project is stored in a GitHub repository and deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud, which installs requirements.txt and runs app/app.py.

5.2 How to build, run and use the application¶

Run locally

# from the project folder (contains requirements.txt, housing_features.py, Sydney_Housing_Data.xlsx and app/)
pip install -r requirements.txt
streamlit run app/app.py          # opens at http://localhost:8501

Deployed version: add your Streamlit Community Cloud link here

Using the app

  1. Choose the suburb and property type.
  2. Enter bedrooms, bathrooms and car spaces.
  3. Enter the land size in m² (enter 0 for units, townhouses or if unknown).
  4. Set the sale date and whether it is a multi-dwelling / development site sale.
  5. Tick the property's features (pool, air con, renovated, views, study, outdoor space).
  6. Optionally paste the agent description; keywords in it (e.g. luxury, development potential, investor) are used by the model.
  7. Click Estimate price to see the predicted sale price and its 80% likely range.

5.3 Reflection on the machine learning workflow¶

Key lessons

  • Data understanding mattered more than the choice of algorithm. The biggest gains came from decisions made in Part 2: modelling log price, treating suburb and property type together, and representing strata land correctly. The three models ended up within about 0.04 log RMSE of each other.
  • Evaluation design changes the conclusions. Ridge looked competitive on log RMSE but worse than the baseline in dollars. Nested, repeated CV and several metrics were needed to see this, and a single train/test split of 101 rows could have produced a different "winner".
  • The largest errors were the most informative part of the project. They exposed a data-coding error (ID 95's Views), a missing value driver (Opera House / Harbour Bridge views), and the structural ceiling of tree models.

Challenges by stage

  • Data collection: manual copying from two portals, prices withheld at the top end, duplicate pastes, an incorrect URL (ID 79), and fields such as floor area and year built that were rarely published.
  • Preprocessing: deciding what "land size" means for strata (complex site area vs. none), filling missing land without leaking information across folds, and handling multi-dwelling sales without dropping below 100 rows.
  • Feature engineering: with only three suburbs, external location data duplicated the suburb label. Text features were useful but blunt, and many were proxies for suburb or type.
  • Model development and evaluation: small folds made hyperparameter choice unstable, and nested CV made the evaluation honest but slow (about 3–4 minutes).

Performance vs. practical deployment The random forest was chosen partly for how it fails, not only for its average accuracy: it never produces absurd predictions, it needs no hand-made interactions, and it is quick to re-train. The cost is that it under-predicts the most expensive properties and is less interpretable than Ridge. The app compensates with ranges, comparable sales and warnings. A deployed version would also need regular re-training as the market moves, input validation, and monitoring of new sales against predictions.

Bias, fairness and limitations

  • Sampling bias: sales with withheld prices (common in prestige markets), different collection windows per suburb, and unequal property-type mixes all shape what the model learns.
  • Fairness: the suburbs differ strongly in income and cultural make-up (e.g. Cabramatta's large Southeast Asian community, Mount Druitt's lower-income profile). A model that learns "suburb = price level" can reinforce existing valuation gaps between communities if it is used to set appraisals or lending decisions, and its errors are not equal across groups (≈ 8% for Mount Druitt units vs. ≈ 30% for Vaucluse houses). Predictions should support human judgement, not replace it, and should never be applied to suburbs outside the data.
  • Marketing bias in text: agent descriptions emphasise positives, and the investor or first-home-buyer language that marks cheaper stock reflects how agents target buyers, not the property itself.
  • Validity: 101 sales from a 17-month window cannot represent the whole Sydney market or future conditions.

Improvements with more data, resources, compute or time

  • More and richer data: hundreds of sales per suburb, more suburbs (which would make distance-to-CBD and amenity features meaningful), and official sales records (e.g. NSW Valuer General) to reduce selection bias.
  • Property-level location and views: geocoding, distance to the water and station, a harbour-vs-ocean view indicator, zoning layers and lot dimensions.
  • Better text and image features: TF-IDF or sentence embeddings of descriptions, and image models on listing photos to capture finish and outlook.
  • Modelling: quantile regression or conformal prediction for calibrated ranges, monotonic constraints (e.g. more bedrooms should never lower the price), a separate model or heavier weighting for the prestige segment, and hedonic models with time effects to track market movement.
  • Engineering: an automated data pipeline with validation checks (e.g. cross-checking Views against the description), a hosted deployment (e.g. Streamlit Community Cloud), and scheduled re-training.
